paras: The killing of Frank Maxwell took place in Augusta, Georgia, about daylight on August 27, 1895, when two city policemen chased and shot Maxwell, a Black convict who had escaped from the county gang. Maxwell died within minutes, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide the same day. The case drew only brief notice in the white press of Georgia and South Carolina.

Maxwell had escaped from the county gang at the junction of Twiggs and Campbell streets and was still wearing the county stripes when he died. The Augusta dispatch called him "a notorious chicken thief" who had been on the gang "more or less for ten or fifteen years."

According to the police account, Policemen Dave Murphy and John Reynolds saw a man hurrying along a dark side street with a bundle on his shoulders. Their orders were to stop such persons, and when told to halt the man ran. Reynolds caught him, and the dispatch said the man "fought him like a tiger" until the officer, feeling himself overpowered, drew his pistol and fired.

The man jumped up and ran; Murphy renewed the chase, and the man hid under a house, was driven out, and fled again. By the officers' telling, he stopped ten or twelve feet from Murphy, shouted that he would kill him, and advanced despite Murphy's order to halt, and Murphy fired. The man fell and died in a few minutes, and only then was he identified as Frank Maxwell.
A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.

The Savannah Morning News carried the Augusta dispatch on August 28 under the headline "Shooting at Augusta. An Escaped Negro Convict Killed by a Policeman." Its account came wholly from the officers' side, called Maxwell "the darkey," stressed his record as a thief, and ended on the jury's verdict. A week later the Manning Times in South Carolina reduced the story to one line in its "News in Brief," crediting Policeman Murphy alone and stating that Maxwell "was resisting arrest."
No Black-press coverage was found, and no account from Maxwell's side or other witnesses appears.

reader.title: Killing of Frank Maxwell
bases: Two Augusta policemen on duty shot a fleeing escaped convict during an attempted arrest, with no crowd involved (A1, A3).
The only detailed report is one Augusta dispatch (A1); the Manning Times brief (A3) is a condensed version of the same police account, not an independent report.

accounts.label: Police account (Augusta dispatch)
accounts.gist: Maxwell ran when ordered to halt, fought Reynolds, who fired; he then threatened to kill Murphy and advanced on him despite an order to halt, and Murphy shot him.

accounts.label: News brief
accounts.gist: Policeman Murphy shot and killed escaped convict Frank Maxwell, who was resisting arrest.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News dispatch presents the officers' version as fact, describes Maxwell as fighting 'like a tiger', calls him 'the darkey' and a 'notorious chicken thief', and closes on the justifiable-homicide verdict.
The Manning Times reduced the story to one line in 'The News in Brief', saying Maxwell 'was resisting arrest'.

record_check.dossier: 1895-08-27: the dispatch is dated Aug. 27 and says the shooting occurred 'this morning about daylight'; Aug. 28 is the publication date.
Black: called 'An Escaped Negro Convict' and 'the negro'.
Policemen Dave Murphy and John Reynolds of Augusta.

record_check.record: Reynolds shot him after a struggle, and Murphy shot him again as he advanced.
record_check.dossier: Reynolds fired during the struggle but the dispatch does not say he hit Maxwell, who 'jumped up and ran'; Maxwell fell and died after Murphy's shot.
Also carried as a one-line brief in the Manning Times (S.C.) on 1895-09-04.

info: About daylight on the morning of August 27, 1895 (dispatch dated Aug. 27, 'this morning')
A dark side street in Augusta; Maxwell had escaped from the county gang at the junction of Twiggs and Campbell streets
Frank Maxwell, described as a 'negro' convict escaped from the county gang, wearing county stripes
Escaped county convict; called 'a notorious chicken thief' who had been on the gang for ten or fifteen years; said to be resisting arrest
Policemen Dave Murphy and John Reynolds; Reynolds fired during a struggle, Murphy fired the shot after which Maxwell fell and died
Justifiable homicide; no report of charges against the officers was found
